tip: 'Andare' plus a past participle expresses obligation: 'queste regole vanno rispettate' means the rules must be respected by all.
'Stare per' plus an infinitive means to be on the verge of doing something: 'sto per partire' = I am about to leave.
'Lasciarsi' plus an active infinitive means letting it happen to you: 'si è lasciato convincere' = he let himself be convinced.
'Nonostante' (despite) requires subjunctive when followed by a clause.
In reported speech, 'ho mangiato' (I ate) shifts one step further back to 'aveva mangiato': 'ha detto che aveva già mangiato'.
'Andare a trovare' someone means to go visit them, not to go find: 'sono andato a trovare i miei genitori' = I went to visit my parents.
'Non mi va di' + infinitive = I don't feel like doing something.
'Basta che' (it's enough that) requires subjunctive.
Italian can front the pronoun and tag the noun on as an afterthought: 'l'ho già letto, questo libro', where the 'lo' squeezed into 'l'ho' points ahead to 'libro'.
'Andare' plus an '-ndo' verb means to go around doing it, ongoing and repeated: 'andavano dicendo' = they kept saying.
'Avere da fare' means to be busy with things to do, not the English have to do of obligation: 'hanno da fare tutto il giorno'.
'Avere' plus a noun plus 'da' plus an infinitive can mean opportunity, not duty: 'abbiamo molto da imparare' = we have much to learn.
Use 'chiedere che' plus the subjunctive when you name who must act: 'ha chiesto che tutti fossero presenti', versus 'chiedere di' plus infinitive.
'Figurati' (informal) / 'si figuri' (formal) = don't mention it, no problem.
'Stavo' plus an '-ndo' verb describes a past action in progress, here interrupted: 'stavo preparando' = I was preparing.
'Mettersi a' plus an infinitive marks buckling down to something: 'mi sono messo a studiare seriamente' = I got down to studying seriously.
'Può darsi' is literally it can give itself and means maybe; 'può darsi che' then takes the subjunctive: 'può darsi che il museo sia chiuso'.
'Finire per' + infinitive indicates an eventual, often unintended outcome.
A direct command in reported speech becomes 'di' + infinitive: 'Vieni!' → 'di venire'.
Time words shift in reported speech: 'domani' → 'il giorno dopo', 'ieri' → 'il giorno prima', 'oggi' → 'quel giorno'.
An impersonal 'è' plus an adjective plus 'che' usually takes the subjunctive: 'è necessario che tutti partecipino', not 'partecipano'.
The subjunctive 'fosse' signals the speaker is not vouching for the claim: 'sosteneva che fosse impossibile' leaves the truth open.
In reported speech a present statement backshifts to the imperfect: direct 'sono stanco' becomes 'ha detto che era stanco'.
'Prima che' requires subjunctive because the event hasn't happened yet.
After 'domandare', a reported question can turn subjunctive: 'perché non fossi venuto', not the plain 'non sei venuto'.
For English 'would come' in reported speech, Italian uses the past conditional: 'ha detto che sarebbe venuto'.
In past reported speech, 'as soon as he had finished' becomes 'non appena avesse finito', paired with 'sarebbe tornato'.
'L'unico che' (the only one who) normally takes the subjunctive: 'l'unico che abbia avuto'.
Front a topic with 'di', then echo it with 'ne': 'di soldi, ne ha fin troppi' = as for money, he has far too much.
'Prima che' takes subjunctive; 'dopo che' takes indicative.
